summary: This proposed standard defines an SMTP extension that lets a message body contain octets beyond the US ASCII range to be relayed over SMTP. This allows 8-bit text to be sent without extra encoding. It was replaced by RFC 1652.

plainLanguage.summary: Old email only handled plain English letters. This extension lets mail servers pass along messages with accented letters and other symbols without scrambling them.

questions: how to send 8-bit email over smtp
subtitle: Lets mail servers send messages with non-ASCII characters without encoding.

tldr.problem: Early SMTP could only send 7-bit ASCII text, forcing non-ASCII content to be encoded before sending, which added overhead and reduced readability.
tldr.mechanism: This extension adds a BODY parameter to the MAIL FROM command so clients can declare whether they are sending 7-bit ASCII or 8-bit MIME data, letting servers that support 8-bit content relay it directly without modification.
tldr.outcome: Servers that support this extension preserve all bits in each octet, avoiding re-encoding overhead. This was replaced by RFC 1652, which consolidated multiple SMTP extensions.

today: RFC 1426 is a Proposed Standard that was replaced by RFC 1652, which consolidated this and related SMTP extensions. The 8BITMIME capability is now part of the modern SMTP protocol used across the Internet.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1426 defines an SMTP service extension that allows message bodies containing octets outside the US ASCII range (hex 00-7F) to be relayed over SMTP without modification. The extension uses the mechanism described in RFC 1425 (SMTP Service Extensions) to negotiate this capability between client and server.

Before this extension, SMTP was limited to 7-bit ASCII content. Any message containing 8-bit data (such as text with accented characters) had to be encoded using MIME transport encodings before transmission, which added complexity and file size.
sections.plainLanguage: Old email servers only understood plain English. This extension lets servers announce that they can handle messages with letters like é and other symbols without changing them.

sections.title: The 8BITMIME Extension
sections.content:
The extension uses the EHLO keyword 8BITMIME to advertise support. When a client wishes to send a message with arbitrary 8-bit content, it first issues the EHLO command. If the server responds with the 8BITMIME keyword, the client can then use an extended MAIL FROM command that includes a BODY parameter.

The BODY parameter takes two possible values: 7BIT (for standard 7-bit ASCII content) or 8BITMIME (for MIME messages with arbitrary octets). When the server accepts a message with the 8BITMIME body type, it must preserve all bits in each octet throughout delivery and relay.

The usual SMTP data-stuffing rules still apply: a sequence like CRLF.CRLF that could prematurely terminate the message transfer is still escaped. Line length restrictions remain in effect (servers are permitted to limit lines to 1000 octets or more).
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks the server if it can handle 8-bit data. If the server says yes, the client announces the type of message it's sending, and the server delivers it without changing the bytes.

sections.title: Fallback When Not Supported
sections.content:
If a server does not support the 8BITMIME extension (either by not responding to EHLO or by omitting the keyword), the client must not attempt to transfer content with non-ASCII characters. The client has two options: first, it may implement a gateway transformation to convert the 8-bit MIME message to valid 7-bit MIME using MIME transport encodings (such as base64 or quoted-printable), or second, it may treat the delivery as a permanent error.

Any transformation must cause no loss of information and must produce valid 7-bit MIME as output. This ensures that even clients without 8-bit support can eventually receive the intended message.
sections.plainLanguage: If the server doesn't support 8-bit messages, the client can either encode the message into a format the server understands, or give up and tell the sender it failed.

sections.title: Usage Example
sections.content: A typical session begins with the client connecting to the server and issuing EHLO. The server responds with 250 8BITMIME among other capabilities. The client then sends MAIL FROM:<ned@ymir.claremont.edu> BODY=8BITMIME. The server accepts this and responds 250 Sender and 8BITMIME ok. The rest of the session proceeds normally with RCPT and DATA commands, and the message content is transferred without any bit transformation.
sections.plainLanguage: The server tells the client it can handle 8-bit mail. The client says the message it wants to send has 8-bit data, and the server says okay. Then they exchange the message.
